summary: This experimental document extends ACME so a server can validate a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Node ID for a client. A Node ID names an endpoint in the Bundle Protocol, so this helps such endpoints obtain certificates.

plainLanguage.summary: Before giving a name badge, the office checks the person really owns that name. This applies the check to nodes in networks where messages may be delayed.

questions: how does acme validate a dtn node id
what is an integrity gateway in dtn
subtitle: How a certificate authority can check that a client really controls a Delay-Tolerant Networking node name before issuing it a certificate.

tldr.problem: ACME was built to validate domain names, but nodes in a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) overlay are named by Bundle Protocol Endpoint IDs, and a certificate authority needs a way to confirm a client controls such a Node ID.
tldr.mechanism: A new ACME identifier type, bundleEID, and a new challenge, bp-nodeid-00, make the ACME server send a Challenge Bundle to the Node ID. The client's Bundle Protocol agent answers with a Response Bundle carrying a digest of a Key Authorization built from two tokens and the client's account key.
tldr.outcome: The document is Experimental. Its authors want feedback on whether the method, multi-perspective validation and integrity gateways are useful in real DTN networks.

facts.label: Response interval limits
facts.value: Not under 1 s; not over 60 s for terrestrial-only DTN

today: RFC 9891 was published in November 2025 as an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says the experiment is meant to learn how useful Node ID validation, multi-perspective validation and integrity gateways are in practice.

sections.title: Why ACME Needs a DTN Extension
sections.content:
ACME, defined in RFC 8555, lets a certificate authority (CA) validate identity claims from a client. It began with domain names, but the document notes the same mechanism can validate any subject identity claim supported by the PKIX profile in RFC 5280.

The claim validated here is a Subject Alternative Name of type otherName with the form BundleEID. It stands for a Bundle Protocol (BP) Endpoint ID in a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) overlay. A DTN Node ID is any EID that can uniquely identify a BP Node, which means it can be used as a singleton endpoint. The Administrative EID is a common choice, and the dtn and ipn URI schemes are valid for it.

The RFC covers the ACME messages, the Bundle Protocol version 7 payloads (RFC 9171) and the Bundle Protocol Security operations (RFC 9172) needed for this. It leaves out how the ACME client or server talks to its own BP Agent, routing of bundles, congestion control and how certificates are deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers live in networks where a message can take a very long time to arrive. They still need ID cards, so this teaches the card office how to check a computer's name using those slow messages.

sections.title: The bundleEID Identifier
sections.content:
A new ACME identifier type, bundleEID, carries a text URI that must be consistent with Section 4.2.5.1 of RFC 9171 and use a scheme from the IANA Bundle Protocol URI Scheme Types registry. An example value is dtn://example/.

The server must decode and normalize each value. A value that fails percent-decoding or does not match its scheme syntax is rejected with the ACME error malformed. A value using a scheme the server does not handle is rejected with rejectedIdentifier. The server must not try to dereference a Bundle EID on its own.

Although a certificate can hold any EID, this validation method works only for Node IDs, which are singleton EIDs. It requires the client's BP Agent to respond to administrative records sent to the Node ID being validated. Non-singleton EIDs are not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The new kind of name is like an address on an envelope. The office first checks that the address is written correctly before it tries to confirm the person really lives there.

sections.title: The bp-nodeid-00 Challenge
sections.content:
The challenge proves control of a Node ID by making the client configure a BP Agent to answer specific Challenge Bundles from the ACME server. It copies the design of the email validation in RFC 8823 and splits a token into parts that travel by different channels.

  • token-chal is unique to each ACME authorization and travels only over the ACME channel, so a DTN eavesdropper never sees it.
  • token-bundle is unique to each Challenge Bundle and travels over the BP channel, so it proves the client received the bundle.
  • id-chal is a random filter value that lets the client's BP Agent recognize valid Challenge Bundles.

Each of these values must have at least 128 bits of entropy and use only base64url characters. The Key Authorization is computed from the concatenated tokens and the client account key thumbprint, and the Response Bundle carries a digest of it.

The client may send an optional rtt hint, in seconds, as a pessimistic estimate of the round trip. The server's response interval should be twice that value, and should not be shorter than one second or longer than one minute (60 seconds) for a terrestrial-only DTN. The server may send several Challenge Bundles, for example over different routes, and each one has its own token-bundle.
sections.plainLanguage: The office sends a secret half-code by post and tells you the other half in person. Only someone who got both halves can write the right answer, so the office knows you are the real owner.

sections.title: Challenge and Response Bundles
sections.content:
Both bundles are ordinary BPv7 bundles whose payload is an administrative record with a new type code, 255. The two kinds differ in a flag: the Challenge Bundle requests user application acknowledgement and the Response Bundle does not. The record content is a CBOR map. Key 1 holds id-chal and key 2 holds token-bundle, both as byte strings. A Challenge Bundle adds key 4, an array of acceptable hash algorithm identifiers in descending preference from the COSE Algorithms registry. A Response Bundle adds key 3, a pair of the chosen algorithm identifier and the digest.

All implementations must support SHA-256, which has COSE value -16. The Response Bundle's source and destination are swapped relative to the Challenge Bundle.

The server accepts a response only if it arrives inside the challenge lifetime, comes from the Node ID being validated, is covered by a trusted Block Integrity Block (BIB), echoes the same id-chal and token-bundle, uses an acceptable hash and carries the expected digest. A missing response is also a failure.

Neither bundle may be directly encrypted. The RFC explains that the challenge is likely sent in plaintext and carries only a random token and a digest, so nothing sensitive leaks.
sections.plainLanguage: The challenge is a letter with a secret number. The reply must copy that number and add a stamp only the real owner can make, and anyone peeking at the letter learns nothing useful.

sections.title: Integrity Gateways and Threats
sections.content:
The RFC defines a Bundle integrity gateway, a routing node that checks a bundle's source by local means and then adds a BIB covering the primary and payload blocks. It resembles DKIM email signing (RFC 6376). The receiver then needs to trust only that gateway, and needs policy for which gateways may vouch for which sources.

The security section walks through four threats. Passive leaks are harmless because the tokens are fresh each time. Node impersonation is reduced by the integrity gateway and by multi-perspective validation, where the server sends Challenge Bundles from several sources or over several paths. A suggested policy is to succeed if the primary source succeeds and at most one secondary source fails. Replay gains an attacker nothing beyond wasted network resources, because the tokens make each Key Authorization unique. Denial of service is handled by ignoring out-of-window or unexpected bundles and by server-side rate limits.

The channels between the ACME client or server and its BP Agent are out of scope but important. If the client sends its account key thumbprint to its BP Agent, that value must be kept confidential.
sections.plainLanguage: A trusted guard at the edge of a neighborhood vouches for who sent each letter. The office can also ask in several ways at once so one trickster cannot fool it.

sections.title: Registrations and Experiment Scope
sections.content:
IANA has added bundleEID to the ACME Identifier Types registry, bp-nodeid-00 to the ACME Validation Methods registry, and the ACME Node ID Validation record type, value 255, to the Bundle Administrative Record Types registry for BPv7.

The Experimental status relates more to the practical value of this validation than to the method itself. The RFC says emerging DTN naming and Bundle Protocol security are still being explored, and that how naming authority is delegated across organizations is not settled. A successful experiment would let certificates be issued across administrative domains, and the authors ask for feedback even from an unsuccessful one.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names and codes were written in the official lists. The rules are still a test run, and the authors want to hear how it goes.
